title: Empowering Local Communities
description: A School, a Forest, and a Tree-Planting Project: The NASCEC-Musunji Partnership
imageCaption: VICE CHAIR NASCEC PLANTING A TREE WITH A STUDENT AT MUSUNJI
content:
Situated on the periphery of a dense forest and adjacent to sacred groves, Musunji Comprehensive School occupies a geography rich in natural heritage. Yet, paradoxically, its own compound bore the marks of environmental neglect, boasting a barely countable tree cover. This anomaly caught our attention. As a local Community-Based Organization dedicated to environmental stewardship, we purposed to adopt the institution as a "model school" for our flagship greening initiative. Our goal was to change the situation; We wanted to create a green space at the school.

The project, however, transcends mere beautification. Recognising the schools strategic location and its simultaneous lack of shade, NASCEC collaborated closely with the Head of Institution and the environmental patron as well as teachers involved with environmental subjects to devise a viable plan. Fruit trees like Guavas, Avocado, Mango and Loquat were intended to supplement student nutrition, fast-growing species like Blue-gum, Gravelia, pine and Cyprus were earmarked for future firewood and timber needs, and indigenous varieties like Mutere, Musizi, and Podo as well as ornamental trees, were planted to restore ecological balance. Furthermore, broad-canopied trees like Acacia were strategically placed to create cool outdoor learning spaces, with all locations carefully mapped to avoid conflict with future infrastructural development.

What distinguishes this initiative is its commitment to participatory learning. In the initial phase, students from lower primary, alongside the entire sixth and seventh grades, took part in the planting and care giving. During the subsequent replanting exercise, known in forestry as "beating-up," junior secondary learners stepped in to ensure the project's continuity. This intergenerational involvement is intended to ensure the schoolyard grows into a living laboratory as years pass by.

The partnership has yielded significant academic insights. In the first phase, nearly 150 saplings were introduced, during the beating-up, 300 saplings were planted, and now a third phase targeting 1000 saplings is scheduled for later this year. Despite initial challenges, such as a lack of protective barricades, which the school later rectified, the survival rate remained impressively good. Notably, the project has uncovered a fascinating variable: soil heterogeneity. Leaching-affected soils from artisanal gold processing facilities exhibit different retention capacities compared to the regular field soils, resulting in varied growth rates among tree species. This discovery has provided both us and the school with a practical lesson in ecology and land management.

To ensure sustainability, NASCEC has assigned field officers, Pauline Minayo and Denzel Luvaha, to monitor growth and report back regularly. This rigorous oversight, combined with the schools active participation, has cultivated a profound culture of environmental agency. The NASCEC-Musunji partnership shows that a simple plan, with good follow-up, can create lasting change for a school. One story, one tree sapling at a time.

title: Innovation Through Technology-(Ecogeim)
description: Code, Culture, and Conservation: NASCEC and EcoGeim's Tech-Driven Environmental Stewardship
content:
Since NASCEC is committed to diversifying how oral knowledge is documented and kept for posterity, at the heart of this mission lies a strategic collaboration with EcoGeim, a youth-led climate innovation platform originally initiated by a group of innovative students at Kaimosi Friends University (KAFU). The partnership between NASCEC and EcoGeim represents a significant expansion of the CBO's working force, enhancing its capacity to fulfil its environmental and cultural mandate. Crucially, a section of the EcoGeim crew are full members of NASCEC, and these members serve as a vital link between the CBO and the broader world of innovators, technologists, and digital storytellers.

EcoGeim's platform combines citizen science, indigenous knowledge, and technology to protect ecosystems and preserve cultural heritage. By enabling communities to document biodiversity, map environmental challenges, record Indigenous Ecological Knowledge, and participate in eco-friendly actions, EcoGeim transforms everyday people into active guardians of nature. The platform employs a range of tools, including environmental education, gamified community engagement, and emerging AI-powered species identification. These technologies are not deployed in isolation; they are integrated with local knowledge systems to ensure that conservation efforts are culturally appropriate and community-driven.

The collaboration is therefore mutually reinforcing. While EcoGeim contributes technical expertise and innovative approaches to data collection and storytelling, NASCEC provides the community networks and grassroots experience necessary for effective environmental action and experimentation. The shared members between the two organisations ensure seamless coordination and a unified vision. This synergy was particularly evident in the recent documentation of indigenous tree species where CBO elders and the innovators worked together.

The ultimate goal of this partnership is to build a future where technology not only protects the environment but also preserves the wisdom and traditions that have sustained it for generations. This is because conservation, as EcoGeim's philosophy asserts, is not just about protecting nature; it is about preserving the knowledge that protects it. NASCEC and EcoGeim are hence demonstrating that environmental stewardship is most effective when it respects and incorporates the wisdom of the past while embracing the tools of the future.

title: Youth and Climate Action
description: Cultivating Skills and Stewardship: NASCEC's Approach to Youth-Led Environmental Engagement Model
imageCaption: Youth Leader Accounting For Trees Planted At Musunji Comprehensive School
content:
NASCEC prioritises youth engagement in environmental conservation. Our approach does not only embed passive learning, but it provides young people with active platforms to apply their ecological knowledge. This practical involvement generates both creative outputs and personal development.

Through our programmes, the youth also share personal narratives, and many of these stories originate from childhood experiences. Some recall being punished for cutting trees or entering the forest without permission. Others draw lessons from quiet, peaceful moments spent observing nature and listening to grandparents' stories. These reflections are not merely nostalgic as they represent real environmental lessons learned at an early age. Currently, two of these collected stories are being developed into documentary projects which will showcase youth perspectives on conservation and the relationship between communities and forests.

NASCEC also values physical wellness as part of our youth engagement. We believe that environmental work requires both mental focus and physical energy. To support this, we recently organised a retreat for our youths, and during this retreat, two teams competed in playful physical exercises. Nonetheless, these activities were designed to promote teamwork, communication, team bonding and healthy competition. These also provided a break from routine work and helped build solidarity among the youths.

Notably, our youth cohort is diverse. It includes innovators, storytellers, and filmmakers. Their ages also vary, as some are still students while others are young professionals already working in their career fields. This diversity strengthens our programmes. It allows participants to learn from each other. We have witnessed students bring fresh ideas while professionals contribute practical experience and the required know-how. Together, they collaborate on environmental projects that combine creativity with practical life skills.

NASCEC's youth model integrates environmental action, creative expression, and physical wellness. By supporting oral and cinematic storytelling, we give young people a voice, and by emphasizing physical health, we ensure they have the energy for sustained advocacy. This comprehensive approach we do believe prepares young participants to become effective environmental leaders in their communities.

title: From Research To Action: The Story Behind NASCEC
description: How a doctoral research project in Tiriki East sparked a community-led movement for culture and conservation.
content:
For centuries, the forests of Vihiga have been more than just trees and wildlife. They have been repositories of memory, where elders pass down wisdom through stories, proverbs, and songs. But as the forests have faced threats from deforestation and climate change, these stories have also begun to fade.

This is where NASCEC's journey truly begins. It starts with a recognition that the decline of our forests and the loss of our cultural memory are not separate crises. They are two sides of the same coin. And if we are to address one, we must also address the other.

NASCEC was born from this insight. A vision that grew out of conversations with elders under the canopy of Tiriki Forest, and the determination of a scholar who saw the connection between environmental degradation and cultural erosion. The vision was simple yet profound: use the power of storytelling to inspire environmental action.

Over time, this vision has taken shape. Today, NASCEC is a community of farmers, teachers, elders, youth, and professionals working together to record stories, plant trees, and educate the next generation. The work is rooted in the belief that indigenous knowledge is not a relic of the past, but a practical guide for addressing the challenges of today.

The results have been remarkable. Students are learning about conservation through the stories of their grandparents. Communities are planting trees that their ancestors would have recognized. And a new generation of environmental leaders is emerging, carrying forward both the wisdom of the past and the innovations of the present.

NASCEC is proof that change is possible when we honor where we come from. It is a reminder that the stories we tell matter, not just for preserving memory, but for shaping the future. And it is a testament to the power of community to rewrite its own narrative, one tree, one story, one generation at a time.
